script:
Chen Meier
Chen Meier was born in the countryside of the Western Gate to a rather poor family. Living in chaotic times, they were often oppressed by local thugs. But Western Gate people valued righteousness, so even thugs would only collect protection fees and not cause further trouble. When Chen Meier was just becoming aware of the world, thugs came to collect money, but her family was struggling and couldn't pay. Just as Chen Meier's parents were pleading with the thugs, several people arrived. Seeing the thugs bullying common people, the young master leading them gave an order, and his men severely beat the thugs, who fled in disgrace. As they left, the men kept praising the young master for his righteous deed and benevolent character, which made Chen Meier happy at the time.
However, Chen Meier's parents looked worried. They told Chen Meier that these wealthy young masters only displayed their righteousness in front of their subordinates and didn't truly care about common people like them. Now that they had offended the thugs, they would surely have no peaceful days ahead. The family immediately began packing, preparing to flee. But soon, the thugs came back cursing and threatening. Her parents quickly told Chen Meier to run away. Chen Meier hid outside until dark before daring to return home, only to find her parents covered in wounds, barely clinging to life, waiting for her return. After saying a few words, they died.
In one day, Chen Meier became an orphan. Living alone made her more mature than others. She would never forget the blood debt of her parents' murder. She worked hard on her own, earned money, hired some people to kill all those thugs, and then began targeting the real instigator—Zhao Zhongyang, the second young master of the Western Gate's Zhao family.
Zhao Zhongyang only used family trusted associates, making him difficult to approach. So Chen Meier used her years of accumulated business experience to join the service of the merchant eldest son, Zhao Zhongzheng. Seeing that she was beautiful, articulate, and seemingly loyal, Zhao Zhongzheng assigned her a task—to use feminine wiles to approach Zhao Zhongyang.
Once she became part of the Zhao family, approaching Zhao Zhongyang became much easier. Through their interactions, Zhao Zhongyang couldn't resist Chen Meier's seduction and fell in love with her. Since they hadn't established a formal marital relationship, killing him wasn't the key—she wanted him to feel the despair of being betrayed by his closest person, and if there was a good opportunity to clear herself of suspicion, that would be even better.
They maintained this relationship for several years, and she occasionally provided intelligence to Zhao Zhongzheng, making Zhao Zhongyang's life less comfortable. In June 1507, Zhao Zhongzheng approached Chen Meier with an abnormal expression, intermittently inquiring about Zhao Zhongyang's recent situation. Chen Meier had never seen the usually composed Zhao Zhongzheng in such a state and realized a storm was coming, so she began formally planning what she had long intended to do.
She prepared a bottle of poison and carried it with her, ready to send Zhao Zhongyang to his death whenever the opportunity arose.
[July 25th]
That night, Chen Meier came to Zhao Zhongyang's room as usual to be with him. Around 11:10 PM, while she was tidying the room, Zhao Zhongyang suddenly screamed. Chen Meier quickly looked over and found Zhao Zhongyang on the ground, clutching his bloody hand which had been pierced through, with a crossbow bolt embedded in the wall.
Chen Meier instinctively ran out to call for help, but suddenly realized—wasn't this a golden opportunity? So she returned to the room, closed the door, walked to Zhao Zhongyang's side, and cruelly pressed on his hand wound. Zhao Zhongyang gasped for air, unable to make any sound, staring at Chen Meier in disbelief.
Seeing Zhao Zhongyang's expression, she finally released the anger she had held for over a decade. Then she took out the poison and poured it into Zhao Zhongyang's mouth, but he struggled and spit it out. So she struck his carotid artery with her palm, knocking him unconscious. Just as she prepared to pour the poison again, she heard footsteps. She hastily hid the poison bottle as the door opened—it was Li Cheng, Zhao Zhongyang's favorite subordinate. Li Cheng frantically checked Zhao Zhongyang and, finding he was still breathing, felt relieved. Then others gradually arrived. Chen Meier deeply regretted her foolish action—when Zhao Zhongyang woke up, everything would be over.
Zhang Wei
Zhang Wei was originally a guard of the Zhao family who, due to his reliable work, was valued by the second young master Zhao Zhongyang and appointed as his personal bodyguard. The Zhao family was a major clan of the Western Gate, and the Western Gate and Eastern Territory had been life-and-death enemies since ancient times.
Zhang Wei loved money. Previously, he worked hard hoping to advance, but now being close to the second young master, he naturally wanted to seize the opportunity to make money. Zhao Zhongyang was the son beloved by the old clan leader, so Zhang Wei believed following him had more prospects than following the eldest son Zhao Zhongzheng. Zhao Zhongyang had two other subordinates: one was Chen Meier, though calling her a subordinate was less accurate than calling her the prospective young mistress, as their relationship was essentially confirmed; the other was Li Cheng, an honest and straightforward man.
Zhao Zhongyang greatly valued righteousness and propriety, which Zhang Wei found somewhat rigid, so he had to rack his brains when wanting to do "business," fearing Zhao Zhongyang's displeasure. Later, he met a "like-minded" friend—Zhao San, a subordinate of the eldest son Zhao Zhongzheng. Since Zhao Zhongzheng was a businessman, he naturally understood that business required some cunning and turned a blind eye to Zhao San's profiteering. Cooperating with him brought much greater profits. Zhang Wei found it strange that sons of the same father could be so different—sometimes when Zhang Wei went too far, he would be severely reprimanded by Zhao Zhongyang.
Once, Zhang Wei was summoned by Zhao Zhongyang because Li Cheng had fallen ill. Zhao Zhongyang personally cared for him and asked Zhang Wei to find the best doctor in all of Western Gate. "Isn't the best doctor in Western Gate the Zhao family's resident physician?" Zhang Wei muttered, but Zhao Zhongyang sat by Li Cheng's bedside asking after his health. Zhang Wei said no more and went to work.
In May 1507, Zhao San approached Zhang Wei, telling him about a big business deal—Boss Ma wanted to buy a prosperous Western Market shop, and they could split 20,000 taels afterward, with Zhao San taking 40% and the rest going to Zhang Wei. Zhang Wei calculated that Zhao San would get so much money just for passing on a message—too good a deal for him. So he pretended to be in a difficult position, telling Zhao San that Zhao Zhongyang was watching this shop closely and he couldn't find a loophole. Such situations occurred frequently, so Zhao San believed him.
After more than a month, at the end of June, Zhang Wei figured Zhao San had forgotten about this matter, so he independently approached Boss Ma and took the 20,000 taels. He greased some palms and sold the shop to Boss Ma. Just as Zhang Wei was celebrating, Zhao Zhongyang summoned him. Zhao Zhongyang looked grim, saying Zhang Wei had caused great trouble—this shop had just caught the family's attention, but Zhang Wei had sold it cheaply for personal gain. When this was traced back to him, combined with his past petty crimes, he would surely face death.
Zhang Wei was shocked and immediately wailed, begging Zhao Zhongyang to show him a way out. But Zhao Zhongyang said he wouldn't protect him. The family hadn't yet discovered his wrongdoing, but Zhao Zhongyang would compile a list of his crimes and report to the family. Zhang Wei was stunned—Zhao Zhongyang could save him, so why was he condemning him to death instead?
This was a matter of life and death, so Zhang Wei had to plan carefully after returning. First, he returned the 20,000 taels to Boss Ma and even added 10,000 of his own, begging him not to reveal his involvement in selling the shop. But Zhao Zhongyang definitely couldn't be bought off. He knew the Zhao family's power and methods well—they wouldn't spare someone who plundered family interests, as it would encourage others to take chances. Even fleeing was impossible. After considering various plans that wouldn't work, Zhang Wei finally decided that only by permanently silencing Zhao Zhongyang and preventing the family from learning of his crimes could he barely survive.
Zhang Wei prepared an extremely fine silver needle, soaked in deadly poison. Just a light prick would kill Zhao Zhongyang without leaving a trace. Now he just needed to wait for the perfect opportunity.
[July 25th]
That night around 11:10 PM, Zhang Wei was resting in his room when suddenly he heard a woman's cry for help from Zhao Zhongyang's nearby courtyard, vaguely saying "the young master has been assassinated." The opportunity had come, Zhang Wei thought, quickly putting on protective gloves, gripping the poisoned needle, and rushing toward Zhao Zhongyang's room.
Many guards also rushed over. As the personal bodyguard, Zhang Wei entered Zhao Zhongyang's room without obstruction and found a crossbow bolt embedded in the wall, Zhao Zhongyang's palm pierced through and useless, unconscious from pain but not yet dead.
Zhang Wei quickly called for a doctor while approaching Zhao Zhongyang's side. Using his body as cover, he secretly pricked Zhao Zhongyang with the needle, then pretended to examine the surroundings, casually smearing the poison from the needle and gloves onto the crossbow bolt. He then walked outside, stuck the needle in the dirt, turned his gloves inside out and stuffed them in his pocket. When he returned to check on Zhao Zhongyang, he had already stopped breathing. Zhang Wei feigned shock and asked the guards who had been watching if anyone had approached—they said no.
acts_goal: Find the real cause of Zhao Zhongyang's death.
